summary: Describes an enhancement to OSPF that lets a router stay on the forwarding path while its OSPF software restarts. This is sometimes called graceful restart or non-stop forwarding. If the topology changes during the restart, the procedure automatically reverts to a normal restart to avoid routing loops.

plainLanguage.summary: When the driver of a bus takes a brief pause, passengers do not all get off. The bus keeps rolling on its route. If something big changes, the trick stops and the usual full restart happens.

questions: how does ospf restart without dropping traffic
what is non-stop forwarding in ospf
subtitle: How an OSPF router can restart its routing software while neighbors keep treating it as part of the network.

tldr.problem: When a router's OSPF software restarts, OSPF normally routes around it while it rebuilds its database, even if the router could keep forwarding packets throughout.
tldr.mechanism: The restarting router sends grace-LSAs that announce a grace period. Neighbors in helper mode keep advertising the router as fully adjacent as long as the topology stays unchanged.
tldr.outcome: If the topology changes, the grace period ends, or a neighbor does not support the feature, the procedure falls back to a normal OSPF restart to avoid routing loops.

facts.label: Grace-LSA type
facts.value: Opaque Type 3, Opaque ID 0, link-local scope

today: RFC 3623 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its procedure builds on OSPF Version 2 as specified in RFC 2328.

sections.title: The Graceful Restart Problem
sections.content:
Many routers separate control functions, such as OSPF routing, from the processors that forward data. That makes it possible to keep forwarding while the control software is restarted or reloaded, which the RFC calls graceful restart or non-stop forwarding.

OSPF gets in the way. Normally it deliberately routes around a restarting router while that router rebuilds its link-state database, by having neighbors reissue their LSAs without links to it. This avoids routing loops and black holes caused by an unsynchronized database. But if the topology stays stable and the router keeps its forwarding tables across the restart, keeping it on the forwarding path would be safe.

The memo adds two ideas. The restarting router originates link-local Opaque-LSAs called grace-LSAs that announce a grace period. During that period its neighbors, in helper mode, keep announcing it as fully adjacent (neighbor state Full), but only while the contents of LSAs of types 1 to 5 and 7 remain unchanged and only periodic refreshes occur. The base protocol is OSPF Version 2 (RFC 2328).
sections.plainLanguage: When a router needs a quick restart, it tells its neighbors to please keep pretending it is still there. If nothing changes while it is away, traffic keeps flowing the whole time.

sections.title: The Restarting Router
sections.content:
To prepare, the router (Router X) must make sure its forwarding tables are up to date and will stay in place across the restart. It must not do the usual shutdown steps, such as flushing its own LSAs, because other routers should act as if it never left. It may also need to keep its cryptographic sequence numbers in non-volatile storage. Without that, adjacencies could take up to RouterDeadInterval seconds to come back, forcing a much longer grace period. The grace period should not exceed LSRefreshTime (1800 seconds).

Router X then originates a grace-LSA on each OSPF interface, with LS age 0 and the grace period in its body, and should retransmit until acknowledged. It records in non-volatile storage that a graceful restart is under way and for how long, then restarts the software.

During graceful restart the router does not originate LSAs of types 1 to 5 and 7, and it accepts its own earlier LSAs as valid instead of flushing them. It still runs routing calculations, which brings virtual links back, but does not install OSPF routes into the forwarding table. If it was the Designated Router on a segment, it elects itself again.

It exits graceful restart when all adjacencies are reestablished, when it receives an LSA inconsistent with its pre-restart router-LSA, or when the grace period expires. On exit it reoriginates its router-LSAs and, where it is Designated Router, network-LSAs, reruns the routing calculation and installs the results, removes stale forwarding entries, and flushes invalid self-originated LSAs and its grace-LSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Before leaving, the router leaves a note saying how long it will be gone and does not tidy its desk. When it comes back it checks that everything is as it left it, then goes back to normal work.

sections.title: The Helper Neighbor
sections.content:
The helper relationship is per network segment. A neighbor Y that helps restarting router X keeps advertising its LSAs as if X were in continuous operation, listing the adjacency to X regardless of its actual synchronization state. If X was the Designated Router when helping began, Y keeps X as Designated Router. One router may help several restarting neighbors at once.

When Y receives a grace-LSA from X, it enters helper mode only if all of these checks pass:

  • Y has a full adjacency with X on that segment.
  • The link-state database (LS types 1 to 5 and 7) has not changed since X restarted. Anything on X's retransmission list must be a periodic refresh, and Y MUST refuse if contents changed.
  • The grace period has not expired.
  • Local policy allows Y to help. Examples are never helping, capping the grace period, helping only on software reloads or upgrades, or refusing specific router IDs.
  • Y is not itself in graceful restart.

Y stops helping when X's grace-LSA is flushed (success), when the grace period expires, or when Y installs a changed LSA of type 1 to 5 or 7 that would have been flooded to X if they were fully adjacent. That counts as a topology change. On exit, Y recalculates the Designated Router and reoriginates its router-LSA, plus the network-LSA if it is Designated Router and the router-LSA for the transit area if the segment was a virtual link. An implementation MAY provide an option to stop database changes from ending graceful restart, though this raises the risk of transient routing loops and black holes.
sections.plainLanguage: Friends of the absent router agree to keep saying that it is still here. They stop pretending as soon as something real changes, because then the old story could send people the wrong way.

sections.title: Compatibility and Unplanned Outages
sections.content:
Backward compatibility with unmodified OSPF routers is automatic. If any neighbor is unmodified or never receives the grace-LSA, it routes around the restarting router, reissuing LSAs without links to it. Helpers read that as a topology change, and the restarting router reads it as an LSA inconsistency. Either way, normal OSPF restart takes over.

The same mechanism can be used after an unplanned outage, such as a crash or an unexpected switch to a redundant control processor. The RFC warns this may not be a good idea, since the router cannot prepare and it is unlikely it could guarantee the sanity of its forwarding tables. Implementations that offer it must let the operator turn it off.

After an unplanned outage the router must originate grace-LSAs after its software resumes, and before it sends any Hello packets. On broadcast networks the LSA is flooded to the AllSPFRouters multicast address (224.0.0.5) because the router does not know its previous Designated Router state. The grace-LSAs go out on all interfaces in Link State Update packets, may be sent more than once, and must carry a restart reason of 0 (unknown) or 3 (switch to redundant control processor).
sections.plainLanguage: If a router never got the message that its friends should cover for it, the friends just carry on as usual and the router does an ordinary full restart. Nothing breaks, it is just slower.

sections.title: The Grace-LSA Format
sections.content:
A grace-LSA is a link-local scoped Opaque-LSA (RFC 2370) with Opaque Type 3 and Opaque ID 0. Its LS age starts at 0 and then shows how long ago the request was made. Link-local scope is enough because only direct neighbors need to see it. DoNotAge is never set, since LS age is used to calculate the grace period.

The body is a list of TLVs, in the same format as the Traffic Engineering Extensions to OSPF (RFC 3630). Each TLV has a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, and is padded to a four-octet boundary without counting the padding in the length. Unrecognized types are ignored. Three TLVs are defined:

  • Grace Period (type 1, length 4): the number of seconds neighbors should keep advertising the router as fully adjacent. Always present.
  • Graceful restart reason (type 2, length 1): 0 unknown, 1 software restart, 2 software reload or upgrade, 3 switch to redundant control processor. Always present.
  • IP interface address (type 3, length 4): the restarting router's address on the subnet. Required on broadcast, NBMA and Point-to-MultiPoint segments, where helpers use it to identify the router.

Additional TLVs must be described in an Internet Draft and are subject to expert review by the OSPF Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The grace-LSA is a short note with three blanks: how long I will be gone, why I am leaving, and which door I will come back through.

sections.title: Suggested Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
Appendix B suggests a minimum set of settings. RestartSupport sets the level of graceful restart support: none, planned restart only, or planned and unplanned. RestartInterval is the grace period in seconds, from 1 to 1800 with a suggested default of 120.

Optional settings include RestartHelperSupport, which takes the same three values for the helper role, and RestartHelperStrictLSAChecking. The latter says whether a helper should end graceful restart when an LSA that would be flooded to the restarting router changes, or when a changed LSA is on the retransmission list at the start. The suggested default is enabled.

The memo also lists a possible future improvement: a less conservative way to end helper mode that gives comparable protection against black holes and routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the dials an operator can turn: whether to allow the trick at all, and how long the router may stay away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A classic attack on a link-state protocol is to inject false LSAs or corrupt existing ones. Injecting a false grace-LSA would let an attacker spoof a router that has actually been withdrawn from service. The standard defense is the cryptographic authentication specified in RFC 2328, and an even stronger option was proposed in RFC 2154.

When cryptographic authentication is used on the restarting router, saving received sequence numbers in non-volatile storage is not mandatory. A replayed Hello packet could cause neighbor state for a deceased neighbor to be created, but the RFC says the risk is no greater than in normal operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake the note and trick neighbors into pretending a router still exists. Passwords and signatures on OSPF messages help stop that.
